content: Ibuprofen is an oral medication classified as a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) with analgesic and antipyretic properties. It is approved by the FDA for the treatment of conditions such as fever, headache, migraine, osteoarthritis, pain, primary dysmenorrhea, and rheumatoid arthritis. Adult Dosage and Indications: For non-prescription use, the recommended dose is 200 to 400 mg taken orally every 4 to 6 hours as needed, with a maximum daily dose of 1200 mg. It should not be used for more than 10 days without a physician's guidance. For osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis, the dosage ranges from 1200 to 3200 mg daily, divided into multiple doses (e.g., 300 mg four times daily or 400-800 mg three to four times daily). Sustained-release formulations, such as 600 mg twice daily, are as effective as regular-release formulations taken more frequently. Doses exceeding 400 mg typically do not provide additional pain relief. The smallest effective dose should always be used. Pediatric Dosage and Indications: For fever in children aged 17 years and older, the recommended dose is 400 mg intravenously every 4 to 6 hours, or alternatively, 100 to 200 mg intravenously every 4 hours, with an infusion duration of at least 30 minutes. For children aged 6 months to 11 years, the oral suspension dose is weightand age-dependent, administered every 6 to 8 hours as needed. For example: 12-17 pounds (6-11 months): 50 mg 18-23 pounds (12-23 months): 75 mg 24-35 pounds (2-3 years): 100 mg 36-47 pounds (4-5 years): 150 mg 48-59 pounds (6-8 years): 200 mg 60-71 pounds (9-10 years): 250 mg 72-95 pounds (11 years): 300 mg Maximum: 4 doses per day. For children aged 12 years and older, the dose is 200 to 400 mg orally every 4 to 6 hours as needed, with a maximum daily dose of 1200 mg. For juvenile rheumatoid arthritis, the recommended dose is 30 to 50 mg/kg/day divided into four doses, with a maximum dose of 2400 mg/day. Studies have shown that ibuprofen at 30-40 mg/kg/day is as effective as aspirin at 60-80 mg/kg/day in managing juvenile rheumatoid arthritis. Warnings and Precautions: Allergic Reactions: Ibuprofen may cause severe allergic reactions, particularly in individuals allergic to aspirin. Symptoms include hives, facial swelling, wheezing, shock, skin redness, rash, and blisters. If an allergic reaction occurs, discontinue use immediately and seek medical attention. Stomach Bleeding Risk: As an NSAID, ibuprofen may cause severe stomach bleeding, especially in individuals aged 60 or older, those with a history of stomach ulcers or bleeding, those taking anticoagulants or steroids, those consuming three or more alcoholic drinks daily, or those exceeding the recommended dose or duration of use. Contraindications: Do not use ibuprofen if you have had an allergic reaction to other pain relievers or fever reducers, or immediately before or after heart surgery. Consult a Physician: Pregnancy and Breastfeeding: Avoid ibuprofen during the last three months of pregnancy unless directed by a physician, as it may harm the unborn child or cause complications during delivery. Consult a healthcare provider if breastfeeding. Adverse Reactions: Common adverse effects include gastrointestinal symptoms (nausea, vomiting, heartburn, flatulence), dizziness, headache, skin rash, and laboratory abnormalities such as elevated BUN, LDH, and platelet counts. Administration and Monitoring: Ibuprofen can be administered orally or intravenously. For oral administration, it is recommended to take the medication with food or milk to minimize stomach upset. Monitor for signs of gastrointestinal bleeding, cardiovascular events, or other adverse effects during use. Storage: Brand Names: Common brand names include Advil, Motrin, A-G Profen, Addaprin, Bufen, Genpril, Caldolor, and Haltran. Patient Counseling: Use the smallest effective dose for the shortest duration necessary. For adults and children aged 12 years and older, take 1 tablet, caplet, or gel caplet every 4 to 6 hours as needed. If symptoms persist, 2 tablets may be taken, but do not exceed 6 tablets in 24 hours unless directed by a physician. For children under 12 years, consult a doctor. Alcohol Precaution: Combining ibuprofen with alcohol increases the risk of severe stomach bleeding. Avoid alcohol consumption while using this medication.
